title: ⭐ Practice: what you like, and how you say it

questions.prompt: Sonia answers: "The lyrics, mostly. I always listen to the words before anything else." Which question was she asked?

options.text: Which song is your favourite?
What do you like most in a hit?
What type of hits do you like best?
Who is your favourite singer?

questions.explanation: "What do you like most in a hit?" asks which part of a song you enjoy, and the lesson gives four possible answers to it: the singer, the music, the melody and the lyrics. Sonia hands back one of the four. A question about the type of hits would be answered by a kind of music — rap, rock, jazz, malouf; a question about her favourite song calls for a title; and a question about her favourite singer calls for a name. Read an answer closely and it gives you back its own question.

questions.prompt: The security officer wants a notice saying that liquids are banned beyond this point. Which notice says it?

options.text: You don't have to take liquids beyond this point.
You mustn't taking liquids beyond this point.
You mustn't take any liquids beyond this point.
You mustn't to take liquids beyond this point.

questions.explanation: A ban is written with mustn't followed by the base form of the verb and by nothing else: you mustn't take. "Don't have to" says the opposite of a ban — it says the thing is merely unnecessary, as in "You don't have to run, we have twenty minutes" — and a notice that says that would let every bottle through. As for the form, a modal refuses the "to" of the infinitive and refuses the -ing just as firmly: he can play, she mustn't be late, never "to play" and never "playing". One rule of meaning, two rules of form, all three in the same short notice.

questions.prompt: A magazine profile of a singer uses four words of the lesson. Match each one with what it means.

options.text: faith
fate
to convene
stardom
the state of being famous as a singer or an actor
what is meant to happen to you, whatever you do
what you believe in, and the trust you put in it
to come together in one place

questions.explanation: One single sound separates faith from fate, and everything else separates them too: faith is what you choose to believe in, fate is what is meant to happen to you whether you choose it or not. To convene has nothing to do with either — it is what a family, a board or a jury does when it comes together in one place, and the word says people, not destiny. And stardom is not talent but what the public has made of a performer: a singer can sing for years before it arrives, and some never see it at all.

questions.prompt: Two words make a minimal pair when ONE single sound separates them and the rest is identical. Which of these is a minimal pair?

options.text: song – sung
melody – memory
singer – single
sea – see

questions.explanation: Song and sung are identical except for their vowel, and that one vowel carries the whole difference — a textbook minimal pair, like them and then or love and luck. The three others fail in three different ways. Sea and see are not a minimal pair but a pair of homophones: nothing at all separates them in the ear, and only the spelling tells them apart, so the count of differences is zero and not one. Melody and memory merely sound close, differing in two places inside the word. And singer and single part company after "sing-", which is one difference too many. Count the differences before you use the term: exactly one, or it is not a minimal pair.

questions.prompt: You are at the check-in desk and you would like to keep a small bag with you in the cabin. Which sentence asks the clerk for permission?

options.text: Must I take this bag with me on the plane?
Can I take this bag with me on the plane?
Can you take this bag with me on the plane?
Must I leave this bag at the desk?

questions.explanation: English asks for permission with "Can I…?", and the subject has to be the person who wants to act — you. "Must I…?" asks something else entirely: whether you are obliged. Asking whether you must take the bag on board is not a request at all, and asking whether you must leave it at the desk settles for the very thing you are trying to avoid. Putting "you" in the question sends the clerk on board with your luggage instead: one word changed, and the sentence stops meaning what you wanted it to mean.

questions.prompt: Tick EVERY sentence that is correct English.

options.text: I'm keen on listening to live recordings.
I'm fond of to sing in the car.
I love to sing in the car.
I'm mad about her early albums.
I'm crazy about to dance.

questions.explanation: Of, on and about are prepositions, and a verb that follows a preposition takes the -ing form: keen on listening, fond of singing, crazy about dancing. Put an infinitive there and the sentence breaks, however natural it sounds in your own language. Like and love are the exception, because nothing stands between the verb and what follows — I love to sing and I love singing are both good English. And mad about a noun needs no verb at all, nor any anger: it says she likes those albums enormously.
